title: The Veil of Ignorance
summary:
John Rawls asked what rules for society free and equal people would choose from behind a "veil of ignorance": not knowing whether they would be rich or poor, what talents they would have, their sex, their race, their religion, or even what kind of life they would want. Nobody could rig the rules in their own favour, so whatever they chose would be fair. Rawls argued (A Theory of Justice, 1971) that people in this "original position" would choose equal basic liberties for all, and allow inequalities of wealth only if they made the worst-off better off than they would otherwise be: they would look at the worst place in each possible society, and choose the society where the worst place is best.

John Harsanyi, who had imagined a similar choice in the 1950s, argued that rational choosers would instead maximise the average, treating every place as equally likely to be theirs. Others choose strict equality. And some critics ask whether anyone can reason at all, not knowing who they are.
citations: John Rawls, A Theory of Justice (Harvard University Press, 1971), §§ 3, 24, 26
